title: ESSAY 6: Demonetisation — Objectives, Impact and Lessons

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: On November 8, 2016, the Government of India announced the demonetisation of all ₹500 and ₹1000 banknotes of the Mahatma Gandhi Series.
The primary objectives were tackling black money, curbing counterfeit currency, promoting digital transactions, and boosting tax compliance.
Demonetisation provided a strong impetus to the digital payments ecosystem, notably UPI, BHIM, and card transactions.
In the short term, cash-sensitive sectors such as real estate, agriculture, and informal labor experienced significant liquidity shocks.
Long-term outcomes included formalisation of the economy, increased direct tax filing, and greater banking sector liquidity.

blocks.content: Demonetisation was a major structural reform aimed at curbing black money, accelerating digitisation, and formalising the Indian economy.

rows: Extremely high reliance on physical currency notes
Structural shift towards digital, cashless, and UPI payments
Lower percentage of population filing income tax returns
Significant increase in taxpayers and direct tax collection
Large shadow economy operating outside banking channels
Higher integration of informal sector into formal banking

items: Frequently tested detail: 86% of total currency value in circulation was rendered invalid overnight on November 8, 2016.
Analytical focus for Mains: Evaluate the dual impact—short-term economic drag on the informal sector versus long-term gains in digitization and tax base expansion.
Key institutions to highlight: Reserve Bank of India (RBI), National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), and the growth of the Unified Payments Interface (UPI).
